messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sokha is a 72-year-old Cambodian American man who has spent the last decade working for a refugee resettlement agency, helping newly arrived families navigate housing appointments, school enrollment, and benefits offices. He had long believed that this work gave shape to losses he rarely spoke about. Last year, while driving a family from his office to a medical appointment, their van was caught near a bombing outside a federal building downtown. He remembers the blast first as force and light: the windshield whitening, then breaking into a glittering spray, the side of the van jolting hard, a child screaming in the back seat. What remains with him most sharply are not ordered recollections but shards—an image of smoke pushing across the street, a man on the pavement with one shoe missing, the red flash of a car alarm, and in his head the layered sounds of the explosion, metal striking metal, horns blaring, people shouting in panic. Even now he says it feels unreal, “like something from television,” and that is part of what unsettles him; he knows it happened, but the memory arrives as pictures and sounds so extreme that he still struggles to believe it happened to him.

In the weeks afterward, those fragments kept forcing themselves on him. At work, if he heard a delivery truck drop its ramp in the alley behind the resettlement office, he would instantly hear the blast again in his head and see the white burst at the windshield. A slammed office door or the metallic crash of a shopping cart outside could bring back the soundscape of that morning with frightening clarity. Because the memory came in these abrupt sensory pieces rather than as a story he could place in the past, Sokha found himself going over the day again and again, trying to make sense of what he should have done differently. He repeatedly blamed himself for taking that route and for being the one behind the wheel, telling himself that if he had left earlier, chosen another street, or noticed something suspicious, the family would not have been there. He also stopped driving whenever he could, and if a colleague offered to take clients instead, he accepted immediately. He became careful about disagreement too; if a client was upset about paperwork or a coworker challenged a decision, he would back down quickly, wanting no escalation of any kind.

Those same intrusive pictures and sounds altered how dangerous the world felt to him. The memory did not stay confined to recollection; it made the present seem poised to break open in the same way. Sokha began to feel safe only in a few tightly defined places—his bedroom, a corner of the family room, and a small office at work if the door was shut. Elsewhere he remained on guard, scanning entrances, listening for changes in traffic noise, tracking who came into the lobby. Ordinary sounds made his body jump before he could think: a bus braking outside, a dropped file, a microwave beeping in the staff kitchen. When he accompanied new arrivals to government buildings, he found himself studying parked vehicles and watching people’s hands instead of focusing on the conversation. What frightened him most was how quickly the sensory memory seemed to prove that danger could appear without warning.

Over the months, that constant watchfulness fed the memories back again. When Sokha was keyed up in public—especially in parking lots, near loading zones, or in traffic—he became more likely to catch a glimpse of reflected sunlight or hear a sharp mechanical noise and suddenly be back inside the van, seeing smoke and broken glass. On days when he was most vigilant at the refugee center, even a raised voice at the front desk could pull the auditory fragments into his mind. The more he limited himself to places that felt controlled and refused rides or driving assignments, the narrower his world became. His supervisor had to reassign outreach visits that required transporting families, a change that embarrassed him and left him feeling he was failing in work that mattered deeply to him. At home, his wife noticed that he insisted on sitting away from windows and avoided any conversation that might turn into disagreement, even over minor family decisions.

He came for help after ducking to the floor at the office when a maintenance cart crashed in the hallway, frightening a newly arrived family he had been meeting with. He was ashamed by how quickly he had reacted and by how little command he seemed to have over his own mind. Sokha says he wants to be able to drive again and to meet families without scanning every sound and exit, but he is afraid that if he lets his guard down, another explosion will come and he will once again be responsible for who gets hurt.
